cards.headline: Boca Raton TLC Program Offers Summer Service Projects for South Florida Families
cards.teaser: B'nai Torah Congregation's TLC Program connects volunteers with hands-on service projects ranging from food support and shoe donations to pantry stocking and literacy efforts.
cards.body:
B'nai Torah Congregation's TLC Program is offering South Florida families a range of hands-on service projects this summer, from food support and shoe donations to pantry stocking, literacy efforts and care for seniors. Led by Summer Faerman, the program connects volunteers of all ages with mitzvah opportunities, or meaningful good deeds, as part of the congregation's broader community outreach efforts.

 The TLC Program stands for Tzedakah, Learning and Chesed, and has made service a central part of synagogue life since 2012. The program provides a way for individuals and families to put Jewish values into action while helping people in need across South Florida. It addresses multiple community concerns including hunger, homelessness, literacy, elder care, vulnerable populations and special needs. Organizers emphasize that the projects are open to everyone in the community, not only members of B'nai Torah Congregation, with the goal of making service practical, welcoming and easy to begin.

 Participants can volunteer in various ways throughout the summer. Projects include making sandwiches, serving meals, collecting and cleaning shoes, stocking Little Free Pantries, preparing backpacks for back-to-school efforts, creating Bags of Hope and helping seniors with technology. Organizers plan to demonstrate volunteer projects such as wrapping presents, making flower arrangements, preparing sandwiches, collecting shoes and assembling supplies for people in need. The variety of options allows families to choose activities that match their interests and schedules.

 As summer continues, the TLC Program offers families a way to stay connected, teach children about giving back and support neighbors throughout South Florida. B'nai Torah Congregation says the program is built around the idea that small acts of service can strengthen the larger community. More information about the TLC Program is available through B'nai Torah Congregation's website.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Food Bank serves 2,500 hot meals daily to children at 35 summer sites
cards.teaser: The Palm Beach County Food Bank in Lake Worth Beach is serving approximately 2,500 hot meals each day to nearly 1,250 children through Florida's Summer BreakSpot program while school is out.
cards.body:
The Palm Beach County Food Bank is serving approximately 2,500 hot meals each day to nearly 1,250 children through Florida's Summer BreakSpot program, according to Food Bank leaders. The nonprofit organization supports more than 35 Summer BreakSpot sites across Palm Beach County while school is out for the summer. During a live Shining A Light broadcast on WPTV, CEO Jamie Kendall and Culinary Director Chef Doug Barg gave viewers a behind-the-scenes look inside the Michelle Hagerty Community Kitchen, where meals are prepared and loaded onto trucks for early morning deliveries across the county.

 The organization prepared more than 36,000 hot meals in June alone. According to the Palm Beach County Food Bank, hunger doesn't take a summer break, highlighting the need for continued support during the summer months. The Summer BreakSpot program provides free meals to children and teens 18 and younger during the summer when school cafeterias are closed. Food Bank leaders said the meals are distributed through partner locations across Palm Beach County to help families facing food insecurity during the summer. Kendall said the Food Bank's partnership with Summer BreakSpot helps ensure children continue receiving nutritious meals while school is out.

 During the broadcast, viewers got a close look at the large-scale kitchen operation responsible for preparing meals daily. Chef Barg walked viewers through the food production process, showing how culinary teams prepare, package and organize meals before they are loaded onto delivery trucks. The loading dock operation featured drivers and volunteers preparing for morning deliveries to Summer BreakSpot sites throughout Palm Beach County. The Palm Beach County Food Bank said volunteers and community support are critical to maintaining the program during the busy summer season.

 The Palm Beach County Food Bank is located at 701 Boutwell Road, Suite A-1, in Lake Worth Beach. Food Bank leaders said the organization continues seeking volunteers, donations and community partnerships to support its mission of reducing childhood hunger in Palm Beach County. Families looking for Summer BreakSpot meal locations can find participating sites throughout the county during the summer months.

hero.headline: Florida leads nation with 12 executions in 2026 as DeSantis oversees record pace in final term
hero.teaser: Florida has now conducted 12 executions in 2026, more than all other states combined, as Gov. Ron DeSantis oversees a record pace of capital punishment at the end of his final term.
hero.body:
DeSantis, who leaves office in January, oversaw a record 19 executions last year, more in a single year than any other Florida governor since the U.S. reinstatement of the death penalty in 1976. Nationwide, the use of the death penalty had been declining for two decades, but that number has ticked up behind the increased pace in Florida. Since 2025 began, Florida has carried out nearly half the state executions across the country. Nationwide, a total of 19 executions have been carried out this year.

DeSantis has rarely commented on the pace of executions, previously noting some on death row had committed crimes as far back as the 1980s. The governor said last year that justice delayed is justice denied and that he felt he owed it to families to make sure executions ran very smoothly. Another execution in Florida is set for August. All Florida executions are by injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.

Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty recently urged DeSantis to halt both executions carried out Tuesday, calling two in one day an unprecedented escalation of Florida's use of the death penalty. Grace Hanna, the group's executive director, said Florida continues to expand the use of capital punishment, despite mounting evidence that it is not what Floridians want. DeSantis has not said why he scheduled two executions hours apart.

cards.headline: Judge keeps Fishback on Florida Republican primary ballot, rejects Collins residency challenge
cards.teaser: Lt. Gov. Jay Collins failed to remove gubernatorial candidate James Fishback from Florida's Republican primary ballot after a judge ruled Collins did not present enough evidence to prove Fishback abandoned his Florida residency.
cards.body:
Circuit Judge David Frank ruled Monday that Collins failed to present enough evidence to overcome Florida's legal presumptions favoring continued residency and access to the ballot. Collins argued that Fishback failed to satisfy the Florida Constitution's requirement that a governor reside in the state for the seven years preceding the general election. Collins attorneys pointed to records showing Fishback voted in Washington during the 2020 presidential election, filed D.C. resident income-tax returns and signed mortgage documents identifying a condominium there as his principal residence.

Fishback testified that he never intended to abandon Florida as his permanent home. He described the Washington property as a second residence or investment and said he signed the mortgage documents without closely reviewing them. Frank acknowledged that Fishback's filings could potentially create legal or regulatory consequences in Washington. But he found that they did not establish that Fishback intended to surrender his Florida domicile. The judge also cited Fishback's Florida upbringing, family connections, drivers license, vehicle registration, voting history and business ties to the state.

The order leaves Fishback on the Aug. 18 Republican primary ballot. Fishback turned his courtroom victory into a campaign counterattack Tuesday, demanding that Collins resign and accusing the lieutenant governor of abusing his office and the public trust by pursuing the residency challenge. Collins rejected the resignation demand and said the ruling would not change his campaign. A Cygnal survey conducted July 12 and 13 placed U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds, the Trump-endorsed Republican frontrunner, at 43%, Fishback at 12%, Collins at 11% and former Florida House Speaker Paul Renner at 2%.

cards.headline: Over 150 assisted living residents remain displaced after Bradenton roof collapse
cards.teaser: More than 150 Florida residents remain scattered across assisted living facilities throughout the Tampa Bay area days after a partial roof collapse forced an emergency evacuation at Aviata at Bradenton Villas early Sunday morning.
cards.body:
Family members and advocates say loved ones have been placed in facilities as far south as Englewood and as far north as New Port Richey, with medical records, wheelchairs and personal belongings still trapped inside the damaged building. George Mendez, who holds power of attorney for 93-year-old Alfred Perani, came to the facility Monday after repeated phone calls to Aviata Health Group went unanswered. Perani, who has been a resident at Aviata at Bradenton Villas for three years, was evacuated to a facility in Palm Harbor. Mendez found an available bed at another facility in Bradenton to bring his friend closer to home but says he cannot complete the transfer without Perani's medical records.

In a joint statement released Monday, the City of Bradenton and Manatee County provided new details about why the Fire Marshal ordered the emergency evacuation. Officials say the partial roof collapse compromised multiple building systems essential to safe operation, including fire protection, electrical and air conditioning systems. Damage to critical support areas necessary for resident care, combined with the inability to safely complete a full structural assessment during the emergency, made it unsafe for residents to remain. The emergency response involved the City of Bradenton Fire Department, Manatee County Public Safety and Emergency Medical Services, and multiple regional partners. All 157 residents were evacuated by approximately 4 a.m. Sunday.

The City of Bradenton is in charge of the building assessment. A city spokesperson confirmed that city officials and the Fire Marshal were on-site at Aviata Monday, along with flooding and restoration specialists. According to the joint statement, the property owner's structural engineer is responsible for evaluating the building, and any determination regarding the cause of the collapse will be based on that evaluation. The Agency for Health Care Administration is conducting site visits at the facilities where residents were relocated as part of its state regulatory oversight.

cards.headline: Florida carries out first double execution in more than 60 years, including second-oldest inmate in U.S. history
cards.teaser: Florida on Tuesday became the first state in nearly a decade to carry out two executions in a single day, putting to death an 80-year-old man who was the second.
cards.body:
Florida on Tuesday became the first state in nearly a decade to carry out two executions in a single day, putting to death an 80-year-old man who was the second-oldest inmate known to receive a lethal injection in modern U.S. history. Dominick Anthony Occhicone was pronounced dead at 6:13 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke following a three-drug injection. His execution came nearly five hours after James Aren Duckett, 68, a former police officer convicted of raping and drowning 11-year-old Teresa McAbee in 1987, received a lethal dose in the same death chamber. Duckett was pronounced dead at 1:19 p.m.

Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has the authority under Florida law to set execution dates, decided earlier this month to carry out both executions on the same day. The lethal injections just hours apart were the first nearly back-to-back executions since Arkansas put two men to death three hours apart in 2017. DeSantis has made Florida's death chamber the nation's busiest at the end of his final term, saying too many families have waited too long to see justice. Florida Department of Corrections records show multiple executions on a single day were more common in the past, the last being in 1964.

Occhicone, who was convicted of fatally shooting his ex-girlfriend's parents in June 1986, is the oldest known prisoner executed in Florida since modern record-keeping began a century ago. Nationwide, an older inmate, 83-year-old Walter Moody Jr., received a lethal injection in Alabama in 2018 for a wave of mail bombs in 1989 that killed a federal judge and wounded a Black civil rights attorney. Asked if he had any final words, Occhicone thanked his Christian brothers for visiting him over the years and apologized to the families of the victims and his own family. Duckett declined to make a final statement.

Florida has now conducted 12 executions in 2026, more than all other states combined. Nationwide, a total of 19 executions have been carried out this year. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, oversaw a record 19 executions last year, more in a single year than any other Florida governor since the U.S. reinstatement of the death penalty in 1976. Another execution in Florida is set for August. The U.S. Supreme Court denied last appeals from both men Tuesday. All Florida executions are by injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.

cards.headline: Poll shows Florida property tax amendment support depends on how voters are informed
cards.teaser: A University of North Florida poll found 61 percent support for Florida's proposed property tax amendment initially, but support fell to 45 percent after voters learned of an estimated $11.8 billion municipal budget shortfall.
cards.body:
A new poll showed Florida's proposed property tax amendment may be popular enough to pass depending on how it is described to voters. The proposal would raise the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes from $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and then to $250,000 in 2028. It would also lower the annual assessment growth cap for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent and restrict how local governments spend remaining property tax revenue.

 The UNF survey initially found 61 percent support after respondents were told the amendment would reserve property tax revenue for core public services. That is narrowly above the 60 percent approval required for a constitutional amendment. Support fell 16 points, however, after respondents were told the proposal is estimated to create an approximately $11.8 billion municipal budget shortfall over two years.

 With that information, 45 percent supported the amendment and 47 percent opposed it. The poll surveyed 848 likely midterm voters from July 8 through July 17.

 Those results add significance to three lawsuits challenging the amendment's ballot title and summary. Plaintiffs argue phrases promising to protect small businesses, ensure fairness and preserve core services amount to political advertising instead of a neutral description of the proposal. The challengers are not asking a judge to remove the amendment from the November ballot.

 If the language is found defective, state law would require Attorney General James Uthmeier to rewrite what voters see. A hearing on the ballot language challenges is scheduled for July 29 in Leon County.

cards.headline: Jellyfish Museum in Pompano Beach showcases medical breakthroughs from ancient sea creatures
cards.teaser: Researchers at the Jellyfish Museum in Pompano Beach have developed an antidote for the potentially fatal sting of the box jellyfish. Other medical advances include collagen harvested from flame jellies that has been found to help stop hemorrhages.
cards.body:
The Jellyfish Museum in Pompano Beach houses thousands of jellyfish in all sizes and shapes, offering a window into some of the ocean's most ethereal and elusive creatures. Naphtalie Jeanty, who holds degrees in both archaeology and anthropology, found her way to the museum through a passion for teaching about flora and fauna. Jellyfish have been gracefully moving through the world's oceans for over 500 million years, making them some of the oldest living species on Earth, predating dinosaurs, trees and even fish.

 Despite the name, jellyfish are not technically fish at all. Jeanty said a lot of the world is starting to describe them as just jellies, and they do not have the same anatomy as fish.

 Researchers at the museum have developed an antidote for the potentially fatal sting of the box jellyfish, which can kill its prey in 3 to 5 minutes. Jeanty said she thinks it is going to be a breakthrough. Other medical advances involve collagen harvested from flame jellies.

 The collagen has been apparently found to help stop hemorrhages, so it might be found in bandages in the future. Research into the Japanese sea nettle has also yielded promising results. There is a part of them that was found to shrink tumors in a mouse cancer, and the next step would be possibly human cancer.

 Jellyfish also perform something called symmetrization, the ability to reorganize their bodies for balance. Moon jellies can regenerate after being split in half, creating two different versions of themselves. Some jellyfish even scrub out microplastics, among the smallest particles of pollution found in seas.

 Polka dotted jellies on display at the museum are native to a lake on the island of Palau in the South Pacific, where they work to keep the lake alive. Jeanty said they provide nutrients and move nutrients all throughout the ocean, taking out excess ones that do not need to be there.

cards.headline: Leon County judge rules James Fishback can remain on Florida governor ballot
cards.teaser: Republican gubernatorial candidate James Fishback will remain on Florida's Aug. 18 primary ballot after a Leon County judge rejected Lt. Gov. Jay Collins' challenge to his residenc
cards.body:
Republican gubernatorial candidate James Fishback will remain on Florida's Aug. 18 primary ballot after a Leon County judge rejected Lt. Gov. Jay Collins' challenge to his residency qualifications. Circuit Judge David Frank ruled Monday that Collins did not present enough evidence to overcome Florida's legal presumptions favoring continued residency and candidate access to the ballot.

 The final order denies Collins' request to remove Fishback, declares that the Department of State properly certified his candidacy and says Fishback shall remain qualified for the Republican nomination for governor. Collins sued Fishback in June, arguing the candidate failed to meet the Florida Constitution's requirement that a governor reside in the state for the seven years preceding the election.

 During an expedited hearing last week, Collins' attorneys presented voter registration, mortgage, tax and homestead records they argued showed Fishback established legal residency in Washington, D.C., between 2019 and 2022. Fishback voted in Washington during the 2020 presidential election, filed D.C. resident income tax returns and signed mortgage paperwork describing a condominium there as his principal residence.

 Frank acknowledged those records could carry consequences outside the Florida candidacy case, writing that the various election and financial filings could result in regulatory or more severe legal repercussions for Fishback under Washington, D.C. law. But the judge found they did not prove Fishback intended to abandon Florida as his permanent home. Fishback testified for several hours that he never intended to move his legal domicile from Florida.

 He acknowledged signing mortgage paperwork identifying the Washington condominium as his primary residence but said he rushed through the documents without reading them closely. He also characterized his 2020 D.C. vote as an inadvertent registration during the pandemic, saying he was staying with his parents and wanted to vote for President Donald Trump.

 Frank found Fishback credible on the central issue of intent. The judge also pointed to Fishback's Florida upbringing, family relationships, driver's license, vehicle registration, voting history and work with Incubate Debate, a statewide nonprofit operating student debate programs throughout Florida. Collins' attorney Mark Meuser criticized the ruling and argued the court improperly accepted Fishback's explanation that he did not understand the legal significance of his Washington filings.

 Meuser did not indicate whether Collins plans to appeal the ruling. Unless an appellate court intervenes, Fishback will remain on the Aug. 18 Republican primary ballot alongside Collins, U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds and former House Speaker Paul Renner.

hero.headline: Martin County projects $16.5 million annual Fire Rescue budget loss under proposed homestead exemption
hero.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue projects its annual budget would decline by $9.5 million in the first year if voters approve expanded homestead exemptions in November.
hero.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue projects its annual budget would decline by $9.5 million in the first year under a proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption. By the second year, the annual loss would reach $16.5 million, a 22% reduction from the department's current budget. Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli presented the planning exercise during Tuesday's commission meeting.

Under the scenario, Fire Rescue could close Station 18 on Britt Road, Station 33 in Hobe Sound, and Station 23 on Kanner Highway. The department could be forced to lay off as many as 116 firefighters by the second year, equivalent to one of the department's three shifts. The funding loss could force Martin County to eliminate specialized teams responsible for hazardous materials incidents, technical rescues and dive operations.

Cianciulli pointed to the deadly Camp Mystic flooding in Texas as an example of delays that can occur when a community must rely on outside resources. In an interview after the meeting, Cianciulli said they had to call for outside assets, a 14 hour response to start mitigating that scene. He said Martin County is in a position where if any incident happens, they are able to do an immediate mitigation without wasting any second.

cards.headline: Martin County commissioners move to rewrite shark fishing rules after public beach complaints
cards.teaser: Martin County commissioners are rewriting rules on fishing from public beaches after complaints that shark fishermen are using drones and remote-controlled boats to drop chum offshore.
cards.body:
Martin County commissioners are rewriting the rules on fishing from public beaches after complaints that shark fishermen are using drones and remote-controlled boats to drop chum offshore and lure sharks closer to swimming areas. County attorneys told commissioners Tuesday that Florida law allows fishing from public beaches and takes precedence over conflicting county ordinances. Commissioners now plan to repeal or rewrite portions of the county's existing law and replace them with restrictions based on public safety.

Some residents said they are concerned fishermen are putting swimmers at risk by attracting sharks close to shore. One speaker told commissioners to imagine going to one of the beaches and taking family while some guy is luring sharks to the shore. Chumming directly from the beach is already prohibited under Florida law, but commissioners heard complaints that some fishermen are using drones or remote-controlled boats to carry bait offshore before dropping it into the water.

County attorneys recommended drafting a new ordinance that complies with state fishing laws while relying on the county's authority to protect public safety and welfare. Under the proposal, fishing could be prohibited from county beaches during lifeguard hours, when swimmers are most likely to be in the water. The revised ordinance would also prohibit fishing from boat docks while boats are being launched or returning to shore. Commissioners directed county staff to draft the new ordinance and bring it back for a future vote.

cards.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue warns station brownouts, higher insurance premiums possible under tax amendment
cards.teaser: Martin County Commissioner James Blake Capps said a no-overtime policy for fire rescue personnel could result in randomized brownouts of stations if the tax amendment passes.
cards.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue projects it could lose 116 firefighters over the next two years about one third of its workforce because of reduced property tax revenue tied to a proposed constitutional amendment on the November ballot. County leaders warned the proposed cuts could lead to longer emergency response times and affect specialized emergency services provided throughout Martin County. Fire Rescue leaders discussed potential operational changes if those revenue reductions occur.

Commissioner James Blake Capps said there would have to be a no-overtime policy for all fire rescue personnel. That doesn't sound so bad initially, but the consequences mean no backfilling of stations with personnel, which would result in randomized brownouts of stations. Capps also said if the county shuts down three fire stations, a lot of people would end up paying more for homeowner's insurance because they would be farther than five miles away from a fire station.

County leaders have previously said the department has few options to absorb the projected revenue loss because about 93% of the Fire Rescue budget is dedicated to personnel. No vote on firefighter layoffs or fire station closures was expected during Tuesday's meeting. Voters will have the final say on the constitutional amendment during the November general election.

cards.headline: Big Taste of Martin County fundraiser to support Big Brothers Big Sisters mentoring programs Oct. 6
cards.teaser: Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties will hold its Big Taste of Martin County fundraiser on Oct. 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart.
cards.body:
Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties is preparing for the return of Big Taste of Martin County, a food and spirits event scheduled for Oct. 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart. The annual fundraiser brings together local restaurants, chefs and community partners to support mentoring programs for children across the Treasure Coast.

 Guests can sample food, wine and beer from area businesses while participating restaurants compete for Big Taste awards and local bragging rights. The event helps fund mentorship opportunities for children who are currently waiting to be matched with a mentor, known as a Big. Spritz Stuart plans to feature several menu items during the event, including a Tuscan salmon dish, a smash burger and a specialty cocktail called the Fig & Flame.

 Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties serves children and families throughout Palm Beach and Martin counties through one-on-one mentoring relationships designed to support academic achievement, confidence and personal growth. Community members can support the mission by purchasing tickets, attending the event or volunteering to become a mentor.

cards.headline: Indiantown Village Council rejects second attempt at data center pause
cards.teaser: Two Indiantown Village Council members failed to convince colleagues to approve a pause on data center applications, with the village attorney warning the move would violate state legislation.
cards.body:
Indiantown Village Councilwoman Karen Onsager moved that the Village of Indiantown establish a 90-day administrative pause on the acceptance, processing and approval of all new applications for large-load data center development projects during the July 13 budget workshop. The motion died after no council member offered a second. Onsager had requested the pause to allow the council and residents to better understand current and projected demands on water and electrical infrastructure through an informational meeting with technical experts, representatives from the South Florida Water Management District and utility providers.

 Village Attorney Wade Vose said such an administrative pause, whether 90 days or 12 months, would violate Senate Bill 180. Vose said he received an email that same afternoon from a local land use attorney who represents multiple developers within the Village, warning that SB 180 would prohibit anything along the lines of a regulation that would inhibit the process of applications for development. Mayor Carmine Dipaolo warned colleagues about offending state officials who have given the village over $120 million in funding.

 The council previously sought advice from Vose last month on a moratorium after scores of local residents protested the village's preliminary review of a data center application submitted by Nelson Ferreira, which he withdrew on April 29. Village Manager Taryn Kryzda confirmed the industrially zoned lands within the village allowed data centers as a permitted use. Onsager confirmed with Kryzda that a community meeting would be scheduled for Saturday, Aug. 2.

cards.headline: Weekend activities include Christmas in July market in Palm City, Stuart Riverwalk concert
cards.teaser: Palm City will host a Christmas in July vendor market Saturday at 2001 SW Murphy Road starting at 10 a.m. The market will feature food trucks, an ornament decorating station and ve
cards.body:
Palm City will host a Christmas in July vendor market Saturday at 2001 SW Murphy Road starting at 10 a.m. The market will feature food trucks, an ornament decorating station and vendors.

 The Downtown Business Association of Stuart is inviting the public to Rockn Riverwalk Sunday at 1 p.m. on St. Lucie Avenue in Stuart. The free open-air concert series takes place every Sunday on the Riverwalk Stage and offers live music on the waterfront.

 Other activities this weekend include the Boynton Beach Night Market Saturday at 5 p.m. at Centennial Park and Amphitheater. The free event connects residents to the local business community with vendors, food and live music.

 A back-to-school family festival will take place Sunday from noon to 5 p.m. at 7715 Forest Hill Boulevard in West Palm Beach. The festival will feature games, food, music and a school supply giveaway.

hero.headline: $70 million K-8 school breaks ground in Fort Pierce, combining three aging St. Lucie County campuses
hero.body:
A groundbreaking ceremony marked the start of construction on a new K-8 school in Fort Pierce that will combine three St. Lucie County schools into one state-of-the-art facility. The new school will be built on land behind Dan McCarty Middle School and is expected to welcome between 1,500 and 1,800 students when it opens. It will consolidate Dan McCarty Middle, St. Lucie Elementary and Lawnwood Elementary into a single campus.

Superintendent Jon Prince said the project is moving forward on time, on budget and on schedule. Prince said the new facility will feature state-of-the-art technology and serve the north part of St. Lucie County. The decision to consolidate comes as the existing schools show their age. All three were built in the 1950s and 1960s. Dan McCarty Middle Principal Latricia Stubbs-James said the wear and tear is visible inside the building and some of the things in there are antiquated.

The district is funding the $70 million project in part by selling the properties where the three older schools currently stand, offsetting the cost of maintaining aging buildings. Prince said the K-8 model is already proven across the district, which operates 11 other K-8 schools. Attendance is better, test scores are better and grades are better in the K-8s, Prince said.

Stubbs-James said the K-8 model offers unique benefits for younger students. Kindergarten students can see what it looks like to be an eighth grader at a new K-8, and what it looks like to be a fifth grader, Stubbs-James said. The new Fort Pierce K-8 school is expected to be completed in August 2028.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce residents oppose proposed mega yacht marina at Museum Pointe over concerns for St. Lucie County Regional History Museum
cards.teaser: Residents and history advocates in Fort Pierce are raising concerns over a proposed mega yacht marina at Museum Pointe, fearing the development could displace the area's cultural heritage and the St. Lucie County Regional History Museum.
cards.body:
The Port of Fort Pierce master plan draft for 2026 calls for replacing the existing area at Museum Pointe with large floating docks designed for mega yachts, along with a clubhouse, an event center and a water taxi connecting to Harbour Pointe to the north. The plan also proposes relocating the history museum. Terry Howard, a passionate advocate for St. Lucie County's history, expressed disbelief over the proposed changes. This is a gem for the area, and I just can't believe they want to put mega yachts here, he said. The museum, it's our culture. It's the center for our culture for this county.

In a statement, St. Lucie County said that no plans have been approved and feedback from the board will dictate future changes, modifications and clarifications to the draft document. Howard has started a petition opposing the proposed marina, hoping to raise awareness and preserve the location and its natural surroundings. This is just a really fantastic place, and our history is capsulized in this museum here, he said. The draft of the master plan is expected to go before the county commission in August.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce police seek help identifying vandalism suspect and vehicle burglary suspects in separate cases
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce police are asking for the public's help identifying people shown in surveillance images connected to two separate investigations involving vandalism and vehicle burglaries.
cards.body:
Police said the vandalism occurred at about 4 p.m. July 24 at the Fort Pierce Recreation Center, located at 903 S. According to the department, an unidentified woman was captured on camera damaging city property. Police said multiple air-conditioning units, a trailer and a storage shed were damaged.

The second investigation involves a series of vehicle burglaries reported during the overnight hours of July 27 in the Lawnwood Circle area. Police said the burglaries occurred in the 1300 block of Nebraska Avenue and the 1300 block of Peppertree Trail, primarily between 2 a.m. Investigators said several vehicles were burglarized. Some had been left unlocked, while others had windows smashed to gain entry. Surveillance footage showed several people in the area wearing hoodies, shorts and backpacks, according to police. Anyone who recognizes the people pictured or has information about either case is asked to contact Fort Pierce police at 772-467-6800 or 772-462-6800. Anonymous tips can be submitted to Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at tcwatch.org.

cards.headline: Man forced to withdraw cash during armed robbery at Wells Fargo ATM in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: A man using a Wells Fargo ATM became the victim of an armed robbery after two men forced him to pull out cash before fleeing the scene on foot.
cards.body:
The Fort Pierce Police Department said the robbery happened Sunday at about 8:38 p.m. Two men approached the victim, and one of them displayed a gun concealed in his waistband before forcing the victim to withdraw an unknown amount of cash. Officers with the Fort Pierce Police Department responded to the scene, established a perimeter, and used a K-9 and drone to search for the suspects.

The suspects were not located. Police described them as two men in their early 20s, about 5 feet 10 inches tall and weighing about 170 pounds. The armed suspect was last seen wearing jeans and a gray hooded sweatshirt.

cards.headline: Three arrested after 3-month-old dies from severe dehydration and malnutrition in Fort Pierce home
cards.teaser: Deputies with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office have arrested three people in connection with the death of a 3-month-old infant, describing the case as one of the worst they have encountered.
cards.body:
The investigation began in August of last year when detectives were called to a Fort Pierce home following the infant's death. The baby had been living with his grandfather, Robert Maxwell, and Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, Vikki Koon, while his mother, Nicole Maxwell, resided with a boyfriend in Vero Beach. According to an arrest affidavit, Koon told deputies she believed a newborn should have two ounces per feeding twice a day. She said when she ran out of formula, she would fill the bottle with regular milk and add water.

Investigators found the mobile home in poor condition. The house was extremely hot. There was a bug infestation in the home, lack of food in the home and the home was unsafe for walking, Detective Corporal Jennifer Diaz said. An autopsy revealed the infant was emaciated and had a sunken abdomen and widespread lesions consistent with severe dehydration and malnutrition. All three suspects are facing several charges, including aggravated manslaughter. Diaz said based on what she observed in her 20 years of law enforcement, this is one of the worst cases she has ever worked.

cards.headline: Two men flee Port St. Lucie officers at 80 mph, one found hiding on roof of occupied home
cards.teaser: A suspected drunk driver fled Port St. Lucie police at nearly 80 mph in a 45 mph zone before he and his passenger abandoned their car and ran, with one suspect later found hiding on the roof of an occupied home.
cards.body:
According to the Port St. Lucie Police Department, officers attempted to stop a white Acura after observing multiple traffic violations and signs of impaired driving. Instead of pulling over, the driver accelerated to nearly 80 mph in a 45 mph zone on Southwest Becker Road. Police said the driver and passenger weaved in and out of traffic, ignored traffic signs and signals, then abandoned the vehicle in a residential driveway near Southwest Idol Avenue before fleeing on foot.

A nearby resident called 911 after seeing the two men run from the scene. Police deployed a K-9 and a drone while officers established a perimeter. Both suspects were located, including one who was found hiding on the roof of an occupied home, police said. The suspects were identified as Joseph Gary Harris, 42, and Bryan Shawn Baker, 46. Harris was charged with fleeing and eluding law enforcement, burglary of an occupied dwelling, resisting an officer without violence, and loitering or prowling. Baker was charged with resisting an officer without violence and loitering or prowling.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie could lose $48 million if property tax amendment passes in November
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie hosted a summer budget workshop as some city council members worry about lost revenue if property taxes go away.
cards.body:
During the workshop, City Manager Jesus Merejo told the City Council the city would lose over $48 million in property taxes over the next two years if the item passes in November. To prepare for the potential hit, the city is holding the line on hiring. Port St. Lucie says it won't fund 184 requested positions, worth $28.3 million, including 25 new police officers and parks staff the city had already planned to add this year to keep up with growth at Torino Regional Park and the new BMX facility at Tradition Regional Park.

City employees also won't get a cost-of-living raise in the coming budget. On the capital side, the $7.8 million in canceled projects includes a study for a new interchange connecting Marshall Parkway to I-95, an inclusive playground at McChesney Park, and parking improvements at Riverland Paseo Park, along with construction on a new City Hall and parking garage. The proposal, known as Amendment 3, is headed to Florida voters on the November 3, 2026 ballot after the Legislature passed it during a June special session. If approved, it would raise the state's homestead exemption from $50,000 to $150,000 starting in January 2027, and to $250,000 in January 2028.

hero.headline: Indian River County Fire Rescue visits Dodgertown Elementary for career fair
hero.teaser: Indian River County Fire Rescue firefighters spent time with students at Dodgertown Elementary in Vero Beach on Tuesday, introducing them to careers in the fire service.
hero.body:
Indian River County Fire Rescue participated in a career fair at Dodgertown Elementary at 4350 43rd Street in Vero Beach on Tuesday, July 28. Firefighters spent time with students sharing what it is like to serve the community while introducing them to the many rewarding careers in the fire service.

Fire Rescue said firefighters answered great questions from students and showed off their equipment during the event. The department said in a statement posted on Facebook that it was a fantastic day of learning and inspiration. Fire Rescue added it hopes to inspire the next generation of firefighters, paramedics and public servants.

The career fair gave students at the elementary school an opportunity to interact directly with firefighters and learn about the various roles available in fire and emergency services. Firefighters were able to demonstrate their equipment and explain how different tools and gear are used when responding to emergencies and serving the community.

The department said its firefighters enjoyed the time they spent with the students during the career fair. Fire Rescue's participation in the school event reflects ongoing efforts by the department to engage with the community and build connections with young people who may be interested in pursuing careers in public service and emergency response.

cards.headline: Recycled fishing line to be transformed into friendship bracelets at Vero Beach Museum of Art
cards.teaser: Discarded fishing line collected from local waterways will be transformed into friendship bracelets during a free Second Saturday program at the Vero Beach Museum of Art on Aug. 8.
cards.body:
Discarded fishing line collected from local waterways will be transformed into friendship bracelets during a free Second Saturday program at the Vero Beach Museum of Art on Aug. 8. The museum is partnering with Coastal Connections for hands-on activities beginning at 10 a.m., including docent-led gallery tours and lessons about protecting local marine life.

 Coastal Connections will lead the bracelet-making activity in the Laura and Bill Buck Atrium using recycled fishing line collected through the organization's Fishing Line Recycling Program. Participants can also learn about the program and marine conservation efforts. The Vero Beach Museum of Art has adopted the fishing line recycling tube at the Riverside Park boat ramp.

 From 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., families can take short, docent-led gallery tours through the Museum Studios family program. Visitors can participate in Nature in Layers, an art activity for children connected to the museum's exhibitions. Guests can also tour the museum's summer exhibitions, including James Prosek: At Work in the Holmes Gallery and Jill Nathanson: Chromatic Phrases in the Schumann and Titelman galleries.

 Second Saturday includes free museum admission throughout the day. Coastal Connections was founded in 2017 with a mission of advancing the survival of sea turtles by educating and connecting people to the environment. Kendra Bergman, founder and executive director of Coastal Connections, said the partnership with the museum is an example of working with the community to introduce marine conservation and environmental protection in unique ways.

cards.headline: Three arrested in Fort Pierce after 3-month-old dies from severe dehydration and malnutrition
cards.teaser: Three caregivers face aggravated manslaughter and aggravated child abuse charges after a 3-month-old infant died from dehydration and malnutrition in Fort Pierce in August 2025, ac
cards.body:
Three caregivers face aggravated manslaughter and aggravated child abuse charges after a 3-month-old infant died from dehydration and malnutrition in Fort Pierce in August 2025, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. Nicole Maxwell, 27, the child's mother, her father Robert Maxwell, 61, and his girlfriend Vikki Koon, 38, were arrested nearly a year after the infant's death.

 Deputies and detectives responded to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital on August 20, 2025, after Robert Maxwell and Koon brought the infant to the emergency room, where the child was pronounced dead on arrival. A medical examiner determined the child died from dehydration and malnutrition and ruled the death a homicide. The infant's ribs were more prominent than its stomach, according to court documents.

 Investigators found the mobile home in the 800 block of Silverstream Circle in Fort Pierce in extreme disrepair. Detective Jennifer Diaz said the home was extremely hot with a bug infestation, lack of food, and was unsafe for walking. Windows were boarded shut, exposed electrical wiring was visible, and live and dead cockroaches were found throughout, according to court documents. Koon told investigators she fed the infant only twice a day and when she ran out of formula, she gave the child watered-down milk with baby cereal mixed in.

 Nicole Maxwell's four other children, ranging in age from 2 to 10 years old, have been placed in foster care through the Department of Children and Families. Robert Maxwell and Koon are being held in the St. Lucie County Jail on $1.5 million bond each. Nicole Maxwell, who was arrested July 23 at a home in the 300 block of 12th Street Southwest in Vero Beach, is being held in the Indian River County Jail on no bond. Detective Diaz said the Department of Children and Families had been involved with the family previously and urged residents to report suspected child abuse or neglect.

cards.headline: Indian River County Fire Rescue participates in career fair at Dodgertown Elementary
cards.teaser: Indian River County Fire Rescue firefighters spent time with students at Dodgertown Elementary in Vero Beach on Tuesday, sharing what it is like to serve the community.
cards.body:
Indian River County Fire Rescue participated in a career fair at Dodgertown Elementary at 4350 43rd Street in Vero Beach on Tuesday, July 28. Fire Rescue said its firefighters enjoyed spending time with students, sharing what it is like to serve the community while introducing the students to the many rewarding careers in the fire service.

 "From answering great questions to showing off our equipment, it was a fantastic day of learning and inspiration," Indian River County Fire Rescue said in a statement posted on Facebook. The firefighters demonstrated their equipment to the students during the event and took time to respond to questions from the children about their work.

 Fire Rescue said it hopes to inspire the next generation of firefighters, paramedics and public servants through events like the career fair at Dodgertown Elementary. The department used the opportunity to connect with young students and introduce them to the various career paths available in the fire service.

 The career fair allowed students to get an up-close look at the work firefighters do and learn about what it takes to serve their community in emergency services. Indian River County Fire Rescue emphasized that the day provided valuable learning opportunities for the elementary school students while also giving firefighters a chance to engage with the community's youth.

cards.headline: Cyclist rides through Vero Beach on 2,600-mile journey from Key West to Maine
cards.teaser: A Boston cyclist rode through Vero Beach this week on a 2,600-mile bike ride from Key West to Maine to honor a friend lost to colorectal cancer.
cards.body:
Jay Weedall traveled to South Florida to begin the journey, with a goal of raising $50,000 for the Young Onset Colorectal Cancer Research Center. Weedall began his journey in Key West, pedaling 155 miles to Miami on day one. He set off on his second leg, a 163-mile ride to Vero Beach, after filling his hydration pack with ice to stay cool.

 Weedall is riding roughly 150 miles a day up the coast through nearly every state all the way to the Pan Mass Challenge. He will do the Pan Mass Challenge across Massachusetts on August 2 and continue to the Canadian border in Maine. By avoiding highways, Weedall says the route offers something unexpected, allowing him to experience little coastal towns along the inlets. Fans can follow Weedall's journey on the cycling app Strava.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Police Department honors service of Indian River County firefighter
cards.teaser: The Vero Beach Police Department said it stands with Indian River County Fire Rescue following the death of Firefighter Geoffrey Lang.
cards.body:
The Vero Beach Police Department said it stands alongside Indian River County Fire Rescue in mourning the loss of Firefighter Geoffrey Lang, who passed away while off duty. The department said its thoughts are with his family, loved ones and colleagues during this incredibly difficult time and that it honors his service and the impact he made on the community.

 Indian River County Fire Rescue announced Lang's death Saturday night and thanked neighboring agencies that quickly shared messages of support following the announcement. The Sebastian Police Department said it stands alongside its brothers and sisters of Indian River County Fire Rescue as they mourn the heartbreaking loss and that Lang's dedication, courage and commitment to serving others will never be forgotten.

cards.headline: Sebastian Police, Vero Beach Police honor Indian River County firefighter Geoffrey Lang
cards.teaser: Multiple law enforcement agencies across Indian River County expressed condolences following the death of Firefighter/Paramedic Geoffrey Lang.
cards.body:
The Sebastian Police Department said it was standing alongside Indian River County Fire Rescue in mourning Lang's death. "Your bravery and service will always be remembered," the department wrote. The Vero Beach Police Department also shared its condolences, saying it stands alongside IRCFR during the difficult time.

 "Our thoughts are with his family, loved ones, and colleagues during this incredibly difficult time," the Vero Beach Police Department said. "We honor his service and the impact he made on our community." Indian River County Fire Rescue posted a photo on its Facebook page Saturday night acknowledging the end of watch for Lang.

 The Indian River County Sheriff's Office also expressed condolences. Anna Kirkland, Indian River Mosquito Control District Seat 2, said she was praying for Lang's family, friends, and the entire Indian River County Fire Rescue family. She thanked Lang for his service to the community.
